youtube_title: Nobunaga's African Retainer Served Him Just 15 Months — Then Vanished: The Real Yasuke
youtube_description:
In 1581 a Black man brought to Kyoto by the Jesuits was presented to Oda Nobunaga. Fifteen months later, the one Jesuit report that follows him places him at the second battle of the day Nobunaga died, then at the mercy of the general who had just killed his lord, and after that the records go quiet. If your lord had just been killed and a church stood nearby, would you have run for it, or walked toward the fighting?

📰 Your reporter: Tokio Kamiya, a former Tokyo foreign correspondent. His grandfather's brass pocket watch carries him to one day of Japan's past at a time. He can watch and he can speak, but he can never change what happens. This time he files his dispatch from Kyoto on June 21, 1582, the morning the Nijo residence fell.

🎌 Subscribe for new episodes 3 times a week:
https://www.youtube.com/@Samurai-Chronicles-JP

🌐 Official site: https://samurai-chronicles.com

🇯🇵 A Japanese perspective on Japanese history — created by a Japanese history enthusiast.

📚 References:
1. Ōta Gyūichi — "Shinchō-kōki" (The Chronicle of Oda Nobunaga), entry for the 23rd day of the 2nd month, Tenshō 9, and the Maeda Family Sonkeikaku Bunko manuscript
2. Matsudaira Ietada — "Ietada Nikki" (diary), entry for the 19th day of the 4th month, Tenshō 10
3. Luís Fróis and Lourenço Mexia — Jesuit letters and reports from Japan, 1581–1582 (incl. Fróis's report of 5 November 1582 on Nobunaga's death), and Fróis, "Historia de Japam"
4. Lamers, Jeroen — "Japonius Tyrannus: The Japanese Warlord, Oda Nobunaga Reconsidered" (Hotei Publishing, 2000)
5. Lockley, Thomas & Girard, Geoffrey — "African Samurai: The True Story of Yasuke, a Legend of Feudal Japan" (Hanover Square Press, 2019), the book at the centre of the modern debate
